title: Short Stuff: Pruney Skin
summary: Short Stuff episode in which Josh and Chuck explore why fingers and toes prune in water. Chuck opens with a story about his daughter soaking in the bath for hours and the wrinkled hand photo that sparked the topic. They explain that the old osmosis theory was wrong, that a 1930s finding about nerve damage pointed to nervous system control, and that the cause is vasoconstriction (blood vessels under the epidermis shrinking) rather than skin swelling. They discuss the 2011 evolutionary theory (Mark Changizi, Boise, Idaho) that pruney skin improves grip on wet objects, a Newcastle study where pruney fingers picked up wet marbles 12 percent faster, and the tire-tread analogy, which Chuck corrects. Josh questions whether the trait must have an evolutionary purpose, and Chuck notes the researchers' view that smooth fingertips may be better for sensitivity and avoiding snagging on objects.

segments.title: Opening and Chuck's daughter's bath
segments.summary: Josh introduces the short episode. Chuck describes his daughter staying in the bath for seven-plus hours and the photo of her wrinkled hand that inspired the topic.

segments.title: Is pruney skin harmful and what causes it
segments.summary: Chuck says the wrinkling is harmless. Josh frames the question of why hands and feet prune in water, especially fingertips and toes. They say the cause was not fully settled.

segments.title: Osmosis myth and the nerve damage clue
segments.summary: Chuck explains that science long believed osmosis caused the wrinkling. Josh describes the 1930s finding that people with nerve damage in their fingertips do not prune, which pointed to nervous system control. They conclude the skin shrinks rather than swells, due to vasoconstriction.

segments.title: Break and the question of evolutionary purpose
segments.summary: Josh introduces the idea that pruney skin may be an evolutionary trait, since the nervous system controls it and that takes energy. Hosts take a break before the theories.

segments.title: Mark Changizi's grip theory and the Newcastle marble test
segments.summary: Chuck describes a 2011 theory by Mark Changizi, an evolutionary neurobiologist in Boise, Idaho, that pruney skin improves grip when wet. Josh describes a Newcastle study in which people with pruney fingers picked up wet marbles 12 percent faster.

segments.title: Tire tread analogy corrected
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the tire-tread comparison. Chuck says the Newcastle biologist's description is wrong, since racing slicks give more grip and treads channel water away, which matches the finger wrinkles.

segments.title: Debate on whether the trait needs a purpose
segments.summary: Josh asks whether pruney skin must have an evolutionary function or could be a byproduct of blood flow shifting away from extremities. Chuck argues advantage is likely, citing foraging and balance examples. Josh says the advantage is not clear. Chuck notes researchers suggest smooth fingertips may be better for sensitivity and avoiding damage.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck wrap up the short with a friendly disagreement, and the iHeartRadio production credit is read.
